title: Why are the Oscars called Oscars? A Hollywood mystery
description: The Oscar’s official name is the Academy Award of Merit. Its nickname has a less certain story, involving an uncle, a columnist and a surprisingly late debut.

sections.title: A very grand prize with a friendly name
sections.html:
Oscar is a nickname for the Academy Award of Merit. The exact origin of the nickname is uncertain. Even the Academy describes the origin as unresolved.

It is a wonderfully ordinary name for a trophy that can change a filmmaker’s evening rather dramatically.

sections.title: Did it look like somebody’s uncle?
sections.html:
One popular story involves Margaret Herrick, an Academy librarian who later became its executive director. Supposedly, she thought the statuette resembled her Uncle Oscar.

The Academy’s own history presents this as a popular story, rather than a proven explanation. An excellent anecdote still needs evidence.

sections.title: The nickname arrived before the paperwork
sections.html:
By 1934, columnist Sidney Skolsky was using Oscar when writing about Katharine Hepburn’s first Best Actress win.

The Academy officially adopted the nickname in 1939. That gap gives us a useful clue: a name can catch on long before an organisation makes it official. It does not tell us who said it first.

sections.title: There is a film reel under his feet
sections.html:
The figure is a knight holding a sword, standing on a reel of film. The reel’s five spokes represent the Academy’s original five branches: actors, directors, producers, technicians and writers.

The name may be uncertain, but the cinema connection is built into the design.
